newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's EMU budget passes, but loose ends remain.
newsitem.headline: Germany's EMU budget passes, but loose ends remain.

text.p: Germany's Bundestag lower house of parliament on Friday passed Finance Minister Theo Waigel's 1997 federal budget into law, putting Germany on course to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Deputies voted by 336 to 313 in favour of the budget, which aims to cut the federal deficit to 53.3 billion marks ($35 billion) from a higher-than-planned 73 billion marks this year.
The total public deficit, taken together with states and municipalities, will be 2.5 percent of gross domestic product and below Maastricht's three percent limit, Waigel said.
"The numbers prove that Germany will qualify for monetary union," he told the fourth and final day of the budget debate.

Waigel's ninth budget, unveiled in July, has had a rough ride through Germany's winding legislative process. It has been buffeted by borrowing overshoots, coalition disputes over tax cuts and emergency spending cuts to cover revenue shortfalls.
The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) kept up their attack on Waigel's credibility, saying that after missing borrowing targets this year the same would surely happen again in 1997.
"None of the country's problems will be resolved by this budget," SPD finance spokeswoman Ingrid Mattaeus-Maier said.

Opposition leaders blamed efforts by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's 14-year coalition to squeeze German finances into EMU's fiscal straightjacket for forcing up unemployment to a post-unification record four million.
In so doing, they hit the weakest point in Waigel's policy: most of this year's overshoot has come from federal transfers needed to top up Germany's underfunded jobless benefits scheme.

Separately, the Bundesrat upper house rejected government measures to save money on unemployment pay and job creation schemes. They now go to into parliamentary mediation, leaving five billion marks in cuts still hanging in the balance.
Matthaeus-Maier also accused Waigel of using the sort of creative accounting which Germany has criticised in other European countries seeking to join the first wave of EMU.

Waigel hit back by saying that his budget would cut back spending by 2.5 percent to 440 billion marks next year, putting Germany on track to reduce state spending as a proportion of GDP to pre-unification levels by the year 2000.

He also rejected criticism of his position on EMU by Bank of France member Jean-Pierre Gerard, who said devaluation of the franc against the mark could become necessary because of Germany's hardline position on an EMU stability pact.
Germany insists European Union members agree on a stability pact that would punish EMU participants who ease fiscal discipline after EMU's start in 1999.

"A European stability pact ensures the stability of the euro. Only a stable monetary union can create economic growth and jobs in Germany and Europe," he said. "Growth and jobs cannot be created through targeted exchange policies."
